result: The gREST_SSCR method was applied to enhance conformational sampling of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein without using predefined reaction coordinates or bias potentials. The method selected eight pairs of charged residues at RBD interfaces as solute regions and performed simulations totaling over 15 μs across 16 replicas, achieving enhanced RBD motions including two-Up-like conformations while maintaining stable intra-domain structures.
evaluation: Claims C23-C24, C32-C36, and C141-C142 collectively describe the gREST_SSCR methodology and its successful application. The method is well-documented with specific technical details (solute selection, simulation length, system size, performance metrics), and the results demonstrate enhanced sampling as evidenced by observation of diverse conformations (C34-C35) while maintaining structural integrity (C36). The approach is validated through citations and computational performance data.

result: The gREST_SSCR simulations sampled Down, one-Up, one-Open, and two-Up-like conformations that agree with cryo-EM structure distributions and smFRET experiments. Principal component analysis showed that PC1 and PC2 capture 85% of conformational variations, with gREST_Down sampling Down to one-Up and gREST_Up covering one-Up to two-Up ensembles. Four major structures were identified with RMSDs of 3.6-5.8 Å to corresponding cryo-EM structures.
evaluation: Claims C25, C29, C37-C51, C110-C111 provide convergent evidence from multiple analyses (PCA, hinge-twist angles, RMSD comparisons) showing good agreement between simulations and experimental data. The quantitative metrics (85% variance captured, specific RMSD values, overlap with 891 cryo-EM protomers) support the quality of the sampled conformations. The monomer simulation (C46) provides additional validation of the conformational flexibility.

result: SASA analysis revealed conformation-dependent accessibility of RBM and antibody epitopes. RBM is shielded by glycans N165 and N343 in Down but increasingly exposed in one-Up conformations, with 1UO showing maximum exposure. Mutational residues K417 and N501 are accessible only in one-Up, while E484 is accessible in both conformations. Class I and II antibodies preferentially bind 1U and 1UO conformations, supporting a conformer selection mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C52-C74 present a comprehensive SASA analysis with consistent findings across multiple conformations and antibody classes. The data show clear trends in accessibility patterns, supported by structural alignments without steric clashes (C65, C73) and agreement with prior literature (C70). The inference about conformer selection (C74) is well-supported by the alignment data, though the functional implications (C55, C57, C59, C61) remain predictions requiring experimental validation.

result: Clustering analysis identified 13 micro-clusters from each simulation that were combined into five main conformational ensembles (DownSym, DownLike, Int2, Int3, 1Up) corresponding to smFRET intensities. The Down-to-1Up transition occurs via four main states including two intermediates (Int2 and Int3), initiated from flexible Down structures with high RBD twist angle variability. HingeA and TwistA are highly correlated (0.94), while HingeA and HingeB show no correlation (0.02).
evaluation: Claims C75-C89 describe a systematic clustering and pathway analysis with quantitative correlation metrics and correspondence to experimental smFRET data (C79). The identification of intermediates is supported by stable basins in free-energy landscapes (C86) and specific hinge angle ranges. However, the classification of I3b as an 'off-target' intermediate (C84) is based on inference from free-energy maps and may require additional validation.

result: Specific molecular interactions drive the Down-to-one-Up transition. Transient salt-bridges between RBDA and RBDC (R408A-D405C, R408A-D406C) lift RBDA from Down to intermediate structures. Glycan at N343B drives the transition by inserting underneath RBDA and changing contact partners, while glycan at N165B acts as a barrier throughout the transition, and glycan at N234B stabilizes one-Up-like conformations.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C90-C94, C121-C123, C126 identify specific protein-protein and protein-glycan interactions supported by contact and hydrogen bond analysis data (referenced in Figure 4). The dual roles of glycans (C121-C123) are inferred from simulation data and consistent with experimental glycan deletion studies (C124). The salt-bridge R408A-D405C is independently observed in other simulations (C120), providing external validation.

result: The one-Up to two-Up transition involves reduced interactions between RBDA and RBDB in one-Up that induce RBDB motions. The transition is characterized by increased contacts between RBDA and RBDC (K378A-E484C, Y369A-N487C, D427A-Y505C) and a slight decrease in RBDA hinge angle in 2UaL and 2UbL. Glycan at N165C acts as a bottleneck, with no specific protein-glycan interactions supporting the transition.
evaluation: Claims C28, C95-C100, C119 describe the 1Up-to-2Up transition mechanism with specific interaction data. The observation that 2UaL and 2UbL are intermediate states (C96) is appropriately qualified as inference. The finding that contacts/HBs are reduced in 2UL compared to 1Ua (C98) supports the proposed mechanism, though the structures differ from full two-Up cryo-EM structures, indicating incomplete sampling of the complete transition.

result: Simulations without glycans show wider conformational distributions and more diverse, asymmetric Down conformations. The transition mechanisms appear similar to those with glycans (RBDA-RBDC interactions), but the two-Up-like distribution connects directly with Down, suggesting loss of structural integrity. Glycans play dual roles in transitions, either helping or hindering Down-to-Up transitions.
evaluation: Claims C44, C101-C104, C114 demonstrate the role of glycans through comparative analysis. The wider distributions without glycans (C101) and direct connection between Down and two-Up-like (C104) are supported by simulation data. However, the inference about 'loss of structural integrity' (C104) and 'dual roles' (C114) are interpretations that, while reasonable, would benefit from additional quantitative metrics or experimental validation.

result: Two cryptic pockets (pocket1 and pocket2) form at RBD interfaces in intermediate structures but not in Down or one-Up. Virtual screening of FDA-approved drugs identified top-ranked molecules including nilotinib, which experimentally reduces SARS-CoV-2 infection by ~50%. These pockets represent potential drug targets to stabilize intermediates and prevent one-Up formation.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109, C129-C131 identify cryptic pockets through computational prediction (P2Rank) and virtual screening. The experimental validation that nilotinib affects SARS-CoV-2 infectivity (C107, C130) provides support, though the mechanism remains unknown. The druggability is supported by binding affinity data (C108) and consistency with prior virtual screening studies (C131). However, the proposed mechanism (stabilizing intermediates to prevent one-Up formation, C109) is speculative and requires experimental validation.

result: The simulation results are consistent with multiple experimental observations: intermediate structures I2a and I3a align with D614G variant cryo-EM structure (RMSD 4.9-5.1 Å); flexible Down structures with asymmetric conformations match mobile RBD observations; glycan roles align with deletion experiments; and antibody binding can be explained by conformer selection. However, three-Up structures were not observed in simulations.
evaluation: Claims C112-C118, C120, C124-C125, C127-C128, C133-C138 provide extensive validation through comparison with experimental data from multiple sources (cryo-EM, glycan deletion studies, antibody binding studies). The consistency across different experimental systems strengthens the findings. The absence of three-Up structures (C113) is acknowledged as a limitation. The inferences about functional implications (C135-C136) are reasonable but remain predictions.

result: Background context on SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, spike protein structure and function, existing structural data, and limitations of previous computational approaches. Over 300 S-protein structures have been determined, showing Down and multiple Up conformations. Previous enhanced sampling methods used predefined reaction coordinates limiting simultaneous investigation of multiple RBDs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C22 provide background information supported by appropriate citations to external data sources (C1), scientific literature (C2-C21), and methodological descriptions (C22). These claims establish context and motivation for the study. The characterization of previous methods' limitations (C20, C22) is based on reasonable inference from the literature.

result: Initial structures for simulations were prepared from cryo-EM structures PDB:6VXX (Down) and PDB:6VYB (Up), with 18 N-glycans and one O-glycan added per protomer based on mass spectrometry experiments and previous computational models.
evaluation: Claims C139-C140 describe the simulation setup with appropriate citations to the source structures and glycosylation data. The methodology is standard and well-documented.
